y1-global: Both examine historical connections and global power; UCR specialises in the comparative expansion, rule and legacies of empires.
y1-ancient: Athenian democracy, social divisions, religion, primary texts and material evidence address an identifiable part of ancient history. UCR does not reproduce the full ancient-world survey.
y1-early: Renaissance Mediterranean art, trade, colonisation and cross-cultural exchange address a substantive part of early modern cultural history. UCR uses artistic evidence rather than the full period survey.
y1-methods: Both investigate historical evidence and the relationship between sources, knowledge and interpretation. UCR focuses on material media technologies and media-archaeological methods rather than the full historian’s toolkit.
y1-modern: Both survey political, economic and cultural change in modern history; UCR is weighted to1815onward.
y2-historiography: Both study how scholarly interpretations of the past and disciplinary methods change. UCR traces art historiography from the sixteenth century onward rather than general historical writing.
y2-gender: Both analyse gender historically using sources and contested perspectives; UCR concentrates on North America from the nineteenth century onward.
y2-lab: Archival inquiry into photographs, news, film and other records contributes directly to historical source research. UCR integrates this with racial and cultural history, participant observation and public media, rather than a dedicated general archive laboratory.
y2-seminar: Both develop focused historical inquiry and source-based interpretation. UCR studies Indigenous histories, colonial institutions and marginalized voices; the relationship concerns historical research, not equivalence to every topic in Radboud’s changing seminar offer.
y3-seminar: Both develop a focused historical research question and an independently researched argument. UCR specialises in modern art and museum histories; Radboud’s restricted seminar topics vary and topic equivalence is not asserted.
y3-thesis: Both formulate historical research questions, critically investigate sources and culminate in a substantial historical paper. UCR’s7.5ECcourse is not Radboud’s required10EChistory graduation essay or a guaranteed archive-based thesis.

blanks.y1-medieval: No selected course establishes a dedicated medieval period survey; isolated medieval material within wider cultural or military study does not supply this component.
blanks.y1-phil: General philosophical reading and art historiography do not establish a course centred on the philosophy of historical knowledge.
blanks.y2-environment: No selected course centres on historical relationships between human societies and the environment.
blanks.y2-minor1: This is a restricted15ECArtsminor package, not a predetermined subject that one selected UCR course can replace.
blanks.y2-minor2: This is a second restricted15ECArtsminor package; package integrity and permitted choices remain distinct from single-course comparison.
blanks.y3-career: Personal development and public-history projects do not establish this History-specific career-orientation course.
blanks.y3-future: Historical visions of the future and public interpretation are present in selected courses, but do not establish the dedicated reflection on historians’ present and future professional role.
blanks.y3-free: Genuine30ECopenstudy outside the own programme has no fixed substantive counterpart.

audience.programmeDescription: History examines change from antiquity to the present and how historians construct accounts of the past. This comparison follows the Dutch-language History pathway in the adopted 2026–2027 regulations.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Both UCR programmes include all six History courses, totalling 45 EC. One emphasises empire and political change; the other cultural history and heritage. Archaeology, art, media and textual inquiry contribute specific historical sources and methods. Shared rows indicate partial relationships, including archival inquiry, art historiography and a substantial historical research paper. UCR does not reproduce Radboud’s full chronological survey sequence or its required 10-EC degree thesis.

curriculum.limitation: The pathway contains 60 EC in each year: 100 EC of compulsory courses, 20 EC of restricted thematic seminars, 30 EC of fixed Arts minor packages and 30 EC of open bachelor study outside the own programme. Mentorship, academic language assessment and personal/professional development include additional noncredit requirements. The ordinary first-year study-advice threshold is 45 EC.

componentNotes.y3-thesis: Required 10-EC History research essay. Entry requires Research Laboratory and one thematic seminar.
componentNotes.y2-seminar: One 10-EC topic from the current B2 seminar offer; Methods and Techniques or Historical Paper required.
componentNotes.y3-seminar: One 10-EC B3 seminar; Methods and Techniques or Historical Paper required.
componentNotes.y2-minor1: One fixed 15-EC Arts minor package; no custom mixing of courses.
componentNotes.y2-minor2: A second fixed 15-EC Arts minor package.

concepts: A programme in history, empire and political change, combining modern, imperial, military, gender and Indigenous histories with political thought, archaeology, art and media evidence. All six UCR History courses contribute 45 EC, including primary-source inquiry and a substantial historical research paper. Related methods and period study provide partial correspondences, while medieval survey breadth and a required 10-EC degree thesis remain different.

A programme in cultural histories and heritage, combining all six UCR History courses with archaeology, art and museum history, intellectual traditions, media and literary interpretation. It offers 45 EC of dedicated History alongside specialist inquiry into material, visual and textual sources. These courses support historical interpretation without reproducing Radboud’s full period-survey sequence or required 10-EC degree thesis.
